catalog-reading-cae-c1-test11-part-1-q1.explanation: C - whileThe word here is used in the meaning of ‘in contrast with something’. The book is not as good as a visit, but it is still worth reading.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test11-part-1-q2.explanation: B - done‘To do a job’ is a common collocation in English

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test11-part-1-q3.explanation: A - gettingAnother collocation, ‘to get up close and personal’ means to get to know something well and thoroughly.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test11-part-1-q4.explanation: B - come‘To come close’ — almost to reach something or to become very similar to. Japanese cars nowadays come very close to German ones in terms of build quality.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test11-part-1-q5.explanation: B - pointA plus point is an advantage, a good or positive aspect of something. Another plus point of learning abroad is experiencing life away from your parents.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test11-part-1-q6.explanation: B - succeeds‘Succeed’ is the only verb here than collocates with the ‘in’ preposition.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test11-part-1-q7.explanation: C - merely‘Merely’ is used as a synonym for ‘simply’ or ‘just’.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test11-part-1-q8.explanation: D - sourceA commonly used set phrase is ‘a source of inspiration’.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test11-part-2-q9.explanation: which/thatIt should be clear that ‘Ping-Pong and Whiff-Whaff’ are the names that imitated the sound. So we use which/that preposition to refer to them.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test11-part-2-q10.explanation: madeA passive voice is used so the verb has to be used in its third form.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test11-part-2-q11.explanation: becameThe word here means that ping-pong have made people crazy about the game.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test11-part-2-q13.explanation: by‘Had already acquired…’ helps to understand that this sentence is about certain point in time.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test11-part-2-q14.explanation: though/althoughDespite the game development, many people still saw it as a simple game for entertainment. Though/although are used in the meaning of ‘in spite of/despite’.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test11-part-2-q15.explanation: rather ‘Than’ that immediately follows the gap is the clue that we should use ‘rather’. ‘Rather than’ is used to show preference. I normally prefer to go outside rather than sit home.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test11-part-2-q16.explanation: against‘Warn against something’ means to inform that it shouldn’t be done.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test11-part-3-q17.explanation: behaviourA noun is needed here. Make sure you spell the word with the letter ‘u’ as it is the correct British spelling

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test11-part-3-q18.explanation: significantThe following noun clearly implies that an adjective should be used here.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test11-part-3-q19.explanation: ridiculousAnother word that is easy to spell wrong. Adverb+adjective pair.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test11-part-3-q20.explanation: numerous/innumerableThe context implies that many studies confirmed the idea that dancing is good for your mood and happiness in general. Note that ‘many’ is incorrect as it is not directly a word-form of ‘number’. ‘Innumerable’ doesn’t fit either because it doesn’t sound scientific, and the whole text is exactly that.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test11-part-3-q21.explanation: Note that ‘efficient’ isn’t right, as this word means ‘performing at the best possible way with the least amount of energy consumed’ and dancing definitely takes more energy in comparison with mimicking or gesticulating, the more widely accepted forms of non-verbal communication. Effective here simply means “successful in producing a desired result.” It is the correct collocation with “form of communication.”

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test11-part-3-q22.explanation: depressionThe word ‘cure’ is a cue to the negative meaning of the word, most likely some sort of illness or state.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test11-part-3-q23.explanation: relationshipsThe reason we use plural form here is because ‘relationship’ in singular normally takes an indefinite article.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test11-part-3-q24.explanation: enabling‘To enable’ means to make something possible, to give right to do something.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test11-part-4-q25.explanation: has taken over the management‘To take over’ means to take control of something owned or controlled by other person.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test11-part-4-q26.answer: no account must this door ever
catalog-reading-cae-c1-test11-part-4-q26.explanation: no account must this door ever‘On no account’ is another way to say ‘never’. Also note the use of inversion.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test11-part-4-q27.explanation: on the recommendation ofTo make more sense of this sentence, imagine there’s an omitted verb, e.g. ‘based on the recommendation… ‘.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test11-part-4-q28.explanation: occurred to us that‘To occur to smb’ means ‘to dawn on smb’, ‘to come to realisation’.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test11-part-4-q29.answer: it made no difference to Kevin
catalog-reading-cae-c1-test11-part-4-q29.explanation: it made no difference to KevinYou can’t say ‘it did not make any difference to Kevin’ only because of the word limit, otherwise it would have been a more obvious choice.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test11-part-4-q30.answer: I might/would be able to make
catalog-reading-cae-c1-test11-part-4-q30.explanation: I might/would be able to makeIt is important to understand the right collocating verb for ‘visit’. ‘Pay a visit’ is used when talking about people rather than places.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test11-part-5-q31.explanation: CLast sentence of the first paragraph mentions that the article on the same subject was read by 30 million people. The article and the book share the same topic and therefore many people are interested in it. Answer A is not mentioned — it is the article, not the book that had been read by 30 million people. Answer B is not mentioned either — the series is dedicated to the idea of different approach to business, not solely to animal behaviour. There is no mention of Answer D at all.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test11-part-5-q32.explanation: AOne but last sentence of paragraph two goes: “… his book is the first time anyone has laid out the science behind a management theory…”. The ‘science’ mentioned here is the evidence from Answer A. Answer B is wrong — even though the book is one from the series, the series is dedicated to business strategies, and only one book of the series focuses on animal behaviour.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test11-part-5-q33.explanation: CParagraph 3 stresses the promptness with which bees make decisions and contrasts it with managers of big companies that take a lot of time to come up with a decision, often not the optimal one. Even though some of the aspects of other answers are mentioned, they are only used here as details rather than the main purpose of the paragraph.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test11-part-5-q34.explanation: C‘Collaborate’ means ‘to work together’. Decision-making as a collaborative process is described in the middle of the paragraph — having a ballot (or a secret vote). Other answers are not mentioned in the paragraph.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test11-part-5-q35.explanation: DThe example of self-organising ants goes to show how freedom of decision-making is beneficial to a company. Answers B and C are not mentioned. The opposite of Answer A is stated — hierarchy ‘gets in the way’.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test11-part-5-q36.explanation: C The only possible difficulty here is knowing the word ‘retain’, which means ‘keep, leave as’. The answer is easily found within the second-to-last paragraph.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test11-part-6-q37.explanation: DSentence 2 of Paragraph A goes ” … with hardly a thought as to what might endure to impress subsequent generations.”; Sentence 4, Paragraph D states the opposite: ” … people have bought and passed on to future generations, those works of art that seemed to embody the spirit of their age and would have lasting value.“

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test11-part-6-q38.explanation: AIn the first sentences of both Paragraph A and C their authors agree that it is very difficult to predict and identify the potential value of a work of art.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test11-part-6-q39.explanation: D Last sentence of Paragraph B states that the works of art can distort the perception of history, giving events of the past more importance than they actually deserve. The second half of Paragraph D is dedicated to importance of art in preserving the history and helping to understand the period it was made in.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test11-part-6-q40.explanation: Only Crouch (Paragraph C) expresses a strongly negative view about the lasting value of contemporary art, stating that ‘mediocrity seems to be the norm’ and that critics risk praising work of ‘merely transitory interest.’ The other historians focus more on the motivations of past collectors or the general difficulty of prediction, without dismissing the potential of current trends.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test11-part-7-q41.explanation: EThis paragraph gives more detail of what is mentioned in the previous paragraph — how Kieron is engaged in drawing. ‘Each one’ can refer to either sketches or his own ‘touches’ — or alterations to the original pictures.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test11-part-7-q42.explanation: GLast sentence of the preceding paragraph helps us here. The authors mentions, that seven-year-old boys don’t give advice to adults on terminology very often, and then Paragraph G explains the situation — “But then Kieron Williamson is not your average boy”. Last sentence of this paragraph goes “my seven-year-old could do better than that” and the following paragraph starts with “Kieron actually can …”.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test11-part-7-q43.explanation: B“Standard seven-year-old boy stuff there” refers to playing football and going to school. This is the easiest anchor that could be used here.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test11-part-7-q44.explanation: DWorld ‘melee’ is essential here to understand connection between the paragraphs. It means ‘a noisy fight, a brawl’ and is used figuratively to describe the situation of immense attention directed towards him.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test11-part-7-q45.explanation: F“Kieron takes it back off me” helps to connect this paragraph with the previous one, where he hands the book to the narrator.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test11-part-7-q46.explanation: C“Michelle Williamson is aware of this” helps to the establish connection with the previous paragraph. She then goes on to suggest how boy’s interests can change and develop as he gets older.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test11-part-8-q47.explanation: BThe development in question is World Wide Web, which is stated in the last sentence of the paragraph.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test11-part-8-q48.explanation: DScience Policy Centre work, journals and discussion meetings are the ways that are meant to make the public more informed on the matters of science.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test11-part-8-q49.explanation: CAn example of young mathematicians from India that had posted result of their research and the rapid reaction to it are mentioned in the middle of this paragraph.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test11-part-8-q50.explanation: CSentence two of this paragraph: “The latter cries out for an informal system of quality control”. This sentence refers to the urgent need to regulate blogosphere that can be a source of all kinds of unconfirmed and even harmful data.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test11-part-8-q51.explanation: ALast sentence of the paragraph mentions Trailblazing website which can be used to access data on scientific discoveries of the past.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test11-part-8-q52.explanation: EMiddle of this paragraph: “Scientists often bemoan the public’s weak grasp of science”

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test11-part-8-q53.explanation: AMiddle of the paragraph describes a “procedure whereby scientific ideas are subject to peer review” that is still used.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test11-part-8-q54.explanation: EFirst few sentences of this paragraph confirm that scientific knowledge and discoveries are not always conclusive and there are certain controversies connected to them.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test11-part-8-q55.explanation: ESecond part of the paragraph talks about involvement of media, politicians and institutions in certain scientific matters, so the issue is no longer purely scientific.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test11-part-8-q56.explanation: DFirst part of the paragraph: “… the widening gulf between what science enables us to do and what it’s prudent or ethical actually to do”.
